text: The tit, building its nest in the mighty forest, occupies but a single twig. The tapir slakes its thirst from the river, but drinks enough only to fill its belly.
note: Contentment with enough; not grasping for more

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting more than they need who could find it is enough.

display_text: The tit, building its nest in the mighty forest, occupies but a single twig. The tapir slakes its thirst from the river, but drinks enough only to fill its belly.
plain: A small bird nesting in a huge forest uses only one twig, and a tapir drinking from a river takes only enough to fill its belly.
core_idea: Take only what you need

text: Now if you have a big tree and are at a loss what to do with it, why not plant it in the domain of non-existence, whither you might betake yourself to inaction by its side, to blissful repose beneath its shade? There it would be safe from the axe and from all other injury; for being of no use to others, itself would be free from harm.
note: Feeling useless; the freedom of not being useful

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels useless who might see freedom in not being useful to others.

display_text: Now if you have a big tree and are at a loss what to do with it, why not plant it in the domain of non-existence, whither you might betake yourself to inaction by its side, to blissful repose beneath its shade? There it would be safe from the axe and from all other injury; for being of no use to others, itself would be free from harm.
plain: If you have a big tree and don't know its use, plant it in the realm of nothingness and rest idly in its shade. No axe will touch it, because being useless to others keeps it safe from harm.
core_idea: Being useless to others can keep you safe

text: Joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, caution and remorse, come upon us by turns, with ever-changing mood. They come like music from hollowness, like mushrooms from damp. Daily and nightly they alternate within us, but we cannot tell whence they spring. Can we then hope in a moment to lay our finger upon their very Cause?
note: Shifting moods and emotions we cannot explain

tags.when_helps: Someone swept by changing moods who is puzzled where they come from.

display_text: Joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, caution and remorse, come upon us by turns, with ever-changing mood. They come like music from hollowness, like mushrooms from damp. Daily and nightly they alternate within us, but we cannot tell whence they spring. Can we then hope in a moment to lay our finger upon their very Cause?
plain: Joy, anger, sorrow, happiness, caution and regret take turns in us, rising like music from hollows or mushrooms from damp. Day and night they change, and we can't tell where they come from, let alone their cause.
core_idea: Moods rise in us from unknown sources

text: To be harassed by the wear and tear of life, and to pass rapidly through it without possibility of arresting one's course,--is not this pitiful indeed? To labour without ceasing, and then, without living to enjoy the fruit, worn out, to depart, suddenly, one knows not whither,--is not that a just cause for grief?
note: Exhaustion from endless toil; life passing too fast

tags.when_helps: Someone worn out by endless toil who wonders what it is all for.

display_text: To be harassed by the wear and tear of life, and to pass rapidly through it without possibility of arresting one's course,--is not this pitiful indeed? To labour without ceasing, and then, without living to enjoy the fruit, worn out, to depart, suddenly, one knows not whither,--is not that a just cause for grief?
plain: Isn't it pitiful to be worn down by life and rush through it unable to stop? Isn't it a real grief to toil endlessly, never enjoy the results, and then leave, exhausted, for who knows where?
core_idea: Endless toil without enjoying life is pitiful

text: Perfect TAO does not declare itself. Nor does perfect argument express itself in words. Nor does perfect charity show itself in act. Nor is perfect honesty absolutely incorruptible. Nor is perfect courage absolutely unyielding.
note: True virtue is quiet, not showy or rigid

tags.when_helps: Someone straining to prove their virtue who might see it needs no display.

display_text: Perfect TAO does not declare itself. Nor does perfect argument express itself in words. Nor does perfect charity show itself in act. Nor is perfect honesty absolutely incorruptible. Nor is perfect courage absolutely unyielding.
plain: The perfect Tao doesn't announce itself. Perfect argument isn't put into words, perfect kindness doesn't show itself in deeds, perfect honesty isn't rigidly incorruptible, and perfect courage isn't rigidly unyielding.
core_idea: The highest things don't show themselves

text: You are going too fast. You see your egg, and expect to hear it crow. You look at your cross-bow, and expect to have broiled duck before you.
note: Impatience; expecting results before their time

tags.when_helps: Someone impatient for results before the work has had time to grow.

display_text: You are going too fast. You see your egg, and expect to hear it crow. You look at your cross-bow, and expect to have broiled duck before you.
plain: You're going too fast: you see an egg and expect to hear it crow, you look at your crossbow and expect roast duck already in front of you.
core_idea: Don't expect results before they can come

text: How do I know that love of life is not a delusion after all? How do I know but that he who dreads to die is not as a child who has lost the way and cannot find his home?
note: Fear of death; questioning our dread of dying

tags.safety_reason: Suggests fearing death is like a lost child refusing to return home, framing death as a homecoming.
tags.when_helps: Someone calmly reflecting on their fear of death, not in distress.

display_text: How do I know that love of life is not a delusion after all? How do I know but that he who dreads to die is not as a child who has lost the way and cannot find his home?
plain: How can I know that loving life isn't a delusion? How can I know that someone who dreads death isn't like a lost child who can't find the way home?
core_idea: Fearing death may be like a lost child

text: Those who dream of the banquet, wake to lamentation and sorrow. Those who dream of lamentation and sorrow wake to join the hunt. While they dream, they do not know that they dream. Some will even interpret the very dream they are dreaming; and only when they awake do they know it was a dream. By and by comes the Great Awakening, and then we find out that this life is really a great dream.
note: Fortunes reverse; life as a dream we may wake from

tags.when_helps: Someone gripped by life's highs and lows who wants perspective on how fleeting they are.

display_text: Those who dream of the banquet, wake to lamentation and sorrow. Those who dream of lamentation and sorrow wake to join the hunt. While they dream, they do not know that they dream. Some will even interpret the very dream they are dreaming; and only when they awake do they know it was a dream. By and by comes the Great Awakening, and then we find out that this life is really a great dream.
plain: Those who dream of feasts wake to grief; those who dream of grief wake to go hunting. While dreaming, they don't know it's a dream; only waking shows it. A Great Awakening will reveal this life as a great dream.
core_idea: Life itself may be a great dream

text: Granting that you and I argue. If you beat me, and not I you, are you necessarily right and I wrong? Or if I beat you and not you me, am I necessarily right and you wrong? Or are we both partly right and partly wrong? Or are we both wholly right and wholly wrong?
note: Arguments; winning does not make you right

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone stuck in an argument who needs to question whether winning means being right.

display_text: Granting that you and I argue. If you beat me, and not I you, are you necessarily right and I wrong? Or if I beat you and not you me, am I necessarily right and you wrong? Or are we both partly right and partly wrong? Or are we both wholly right and wholly wrong?
plain: Suppose you and I argue. If you win, are you necessarily right and I wrong, or the other way round? Or are we each partly right and partly wrong, or both entirely right or entirely wrong?
core_idea: Winning an argument doesn't prove you right

text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
note: Uncertainty about identity and what is real

tags.when_helps: Someone questioning who they really are, open to wonder rather than answers.

display_text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
plain: Chuang Tzu dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering about, unaware of being a man. He woke as himself, and now can't tell if he was a man dreaming he was a butterfly, or is a butterfly dreaming he's a man.
core_idea: Am I a man or a dreaming butterfly?

text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
note: Overreaching; accepting the limits of one life

tags.when_helps: Someone exhausting themselves trying to know everything.

display_text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
plain: My life is limited, but knowledge has no limit. Using what is limited to chase what is limitless is ruinous, and those who try it lose themselves.
core_idea: Chasing limitless knowledge with a limited life ruins you

plain_judge.issue: Softens 'fatal' to 'ruinous'; 'knowledge fatally lost' becomes 'lose themselves'.

text: In striving for others, avoid fame. In striving for self, avoid disgrace. Pursue a middle course. Thus you will keep a sound body, and a sound mind, fulfil your duties, and work out your allotted span.
note: Balance and moderation in work and ambition

tags.when_helps: Someone pulled between ambition and caution who wants a balanced path.

display_text: In striving for others, avoid fame. In striving for self, avoid disgrace. Pursue a middle course. Thus you will keep a sound body, and a sound mind, fulfil your duties, and work out your allotted span.
plain: When you work for others, don't chase fame; when you work for yourself, avoid shame. Keep to the middle way, and you will stay healthy in body and mind, do your duties, and live out your natural life.
core_idea: Keep to the middle way, avoiding fame and disgrace

text: A good cook changes his chopper once a year,--because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,--because he hacks. But I have had this chopper nineteen years, and although I have cut up many thousand bullocks, its edge is as if fresh from the whetstone.
note: Working with ease instead of force; avoiding burnout

tags.when_helps: Someone forcing their way through work who could find an easier, skilful way.

display_text: A good cook changes his chopper once a year,--because he cuts. An ordinary cook, once a month,--because he hacks. But I have had this chopper nineteen years, and although I have cut up many thousand bullocks, its edge is as if fresh from the whetstone.
plain: A good cook replaces his knife yearly because he slices; an ordinary cook monthly because he hacks. This cook has used one knife for nineteen years on thousands of oxen, and it is still as sharp as new.
core_idea: Skill that works with things wears nothing out

text: Now, wild fowl get a peck once in ten steps, a drink once in a hundred. Yet they do not want to be fed in a cage. For although they would thus be able to command food, they would not be free.
note: Choosing freedom over comfortable security

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing security against freedom, such as a comfortable but confining job.

display_text: Now, wild fowl get a peck once in ten steps, a drink once in a hundred. Yet they do not want to be fed in a cage. For although they would thus be able to command food, they would not be free.
plain: Wild birds have to search hard for every bite and every drink, yet they don't want to be fed in a cage. In a cage they would have food on demand, but they would not be free.
core_idea: Freedom is worth more than easy comfort

text: The Master came, because it was his time to be born; he went, because it was his time to die. For those who accept the phenomenon of birth and death in this sense, lamentation and sorrow have no place. The ancients spoke of death as of God cutting down a man suspended in the air. The fuel is consumed, but the fire may be transmitted, and we know not that it comes to an end.
note: Grief; accepting death as part of a natural course

tags.when_helps: Someone mourning a death who seeks a way to accept birth and death as natural.

display_text: The Master came, because it was his time to be born; he went, because it was his time to die. For those who accept the phenomenon of birth and death in this sense, lamentation and sorrow have no place. The ancients spoke of death as of God cutting down a man suspended in the air. The fuel is consumed, but the fire may be transmitted, and we know not that it comes to an end.
plain: The Master was born when his time came and died when his time came. Accept birth and death like that, and grief has no place. The fuel burns out, but the fire may pass on endlessly.
core_idea: Accepting birth and death in their time ends grief

plain_judge.issue: 'Pass on endlessly' overstates 'we know not that it comes to an end'.

text: The sages of old first got TAO for themselves, and then got it for others. Before you possess this yourself, what leisure have you to attend to the doings of wicked men?
note: Fixing yourself before trying to fix others

tags.when_helps: Someone eager to fix others' wrongs before tending their own growth.

display_text: The sages of old first got TAO for themselves, and then got it for others. Before you possess this yourself, what leisure have you to attend to the doings of wicked men?
plain: The wise people of old first found the Tao for themselves and only then shared it with others. Until you have it yourself, you have no time to spare for dealing with what wicked people do.
core_idea: Find the Tao yourself before trying to fix others

text: You hear not with the ears, but with the mind; not with the mind, but with your soul. But let hearing stop with the ears. Let the working of the mind stop with itself. Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only TAO can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart.
note: Stilling the mind; inner emptiness as spiritual practice

tags.when_helps: Someone with a busy mind seeking a contemplative way to quiet it.

display_text: You hear not with the ears, but with the mind; not with the mind, but with your soul. But let hearing stop with the ears. Let the working of the mind stop with itself. Then the soul will be a negative existence, passively responsive to externals. In such a negative existence, only TAO can abide. And that negative state is the fasting of the heart.
plain: Listen not with your ears or mind but with your soul. Let hearing and thinking stop, so the soul is empty and simply responds. Only the Tao lives in that emptiness; this is fasting of the heart.
core_idea: An empty, receptive heart is where the Tao lives

text: To serve one's own heart so as to permit neither joy nor sorrow within, but to cultivate resignation to the inevitable,--this is the climax of Virtue.
note: Accepting what cannot be changed; inner steadiness

tags.when_helps: Someone tossed between highs and lows who wants to accept what cannot change.

display_text: To serve one's own heart so as to permit neither joy nor sorrow within, but to cultivate resignation to the inevitable,--this is the climax of Virtue.
plain: The highest virtue is to tend your own heart so that neither joy nor sorrow takes hold of it, and to learn to accept what cannot be avoided.
core_idea: Highest virtue is calm acceptance of the inevitable

text: Now a minister often finds himself in circumstances over which he has no control. But if he simply confines himself to his work, and is utterly oblivious of self, what leisure has he for loving life or hating death?
note: Work anxiety; focusing on the task, not outcomes

tags.when_helps: Someone in a work situation beyond their control who needs to focus on the task.

display_text: Now a minister often finds himself in circumstances over which he has no control. But if he simply confines himself to his work, and is utterly oblivious of self, what leisure has he for loving life or hating death?
plain: An official often faces situations he cannot control. But if he simply sticks to his work and forgets himself completely, he has no time left to cling to life or dread death.
core_idea: Absorption in your work frees you from fear of death

text: In trials of skill, at first all is friendliness; but at last it is all antagonism. Skill is pushed too far. So on festive occasions, the drinking which is in the beginning orderly enough, degenerates into riot and disorder. Festivity is pushed too far. It is in fact the same with all things: they begin with good faith and end with contempt. From small beginnings come great endings.
note: Things going too far; good starts turning sour

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone watching a friendly rivalry or celebration slide into conflict.

display_text: In trials of skill, at first all is friendliness; but at last it is all antagonism. Skill is pushed too far. So on festive occasions, the drinking which is in the beginning orderly enough, degenerates into riot and disorder. Festivity is pushed too far. It is in fact the same with all things: they begin with good faith and end with contempt. From small beginnings come great endings.
plain: Contests start friendly and end hostile; parties start orderly and end in drunken chaos, because things are pushed too far. Everything is like this: it begins in good faith and ends in contempt. Small beginnings lead to big endings.
core_idea: Things pushed too far turn from good faith to contempt

text: Speech is like wind to wave. Action is liable to divergence from its true goal. By wind, waves are easily excited. Divergence from the true goal is fraught with danger. Thus angry feelings rise up without a cause. Specious words and dishonest arguments follow, as the wild random cries of an animal at the point of death. Both sides give way to passion. For where one party drives the other too much into a corner, resistance will always be provoked without apparent cause.
note: How words escalate conflict and anger

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone in a heated dispute who should avoid pushing the other side into a corner.

display_text: Speech is like wind to wave. Action is liable to divergence from its true goal. By wind, waves are easily excited. Divergence from the true goal is fraught with danger. Thus angry feelings rise up without a cause. Specious words and dishonest arguments follow, as the wild random cries of an animal at the point of death. Both sides give way to passion. For where one party drives the other too much into a corner, resistance will always be provoked without apparent cause.
plain: Words stir people up as wind stirs waves, and actions easily drift from their aim. So anger flares for no clear reason, and dishonest arguments follow. When you push someone too far into a corner, they will always fight back.
core_idea: Push someone into a corner and they will resist

plain_judge.issue: Drops that both sides give way to passion; loses the dying-animal image.

text: Don't you know the story of the praying mantis? In its rage it stretched out its arms to prevent a chariot from passing, unaware that this was beyond its strength, so admirable was its energy! Be cautious. If you are always offending others by your superiority, you will probably come to grief.
note: Overestimating yourself; arrogance and picking hopeless fights

tags.when_helps: Someone about to take on a fight beyond their strength out of pride.

display_text: Don't you know the story of the praying mantis? In its rage it stretched out its arms to prevent a chariot from passing, unaware that this was beyond its strength, so admirable was its energy! Be cautious. If you are always offending others by your superiority, you will probably come to grief.
plain: The praying mantis raised its arms to stop a chariot, not knowing it was far too weak, so proud was it of its energy. Be careful: if you keep offending people by acting superior, you will probably come to harm.
core_idea: Showing off your superiority leads to harm

text: Those who are fond of horses surround them with various conveniences. Sometimes mosquitoes or flies trouble them; and then, unexpectedly to the animal, a groom will brush them off, the result being that the horse breaks his bridle, and hurts his head and chest. The intention is good, but there is a want of real care for the horse.
note: Well-meant help that harms; real care for others

situations: caring for a sick or ageing relative
tags.when_helps: A carer whose well-meant help is backfiring and needs gentler attention.

display_text: Those who are fond of horses surround them with various conveniences. Sometimes mosquitoes or flies trouble them; and then, unexpectedly to the animal, a groom will brush them off, the result being that the horse breaks his bridle, and hurts his head and chest. The intention is good, but there is a want of real care for the horse.
plain: People who love horses pamper them. But when a groom suddenly swats a fly off a horse, the startled animal breaks its bridle and hurts itself. The intention is good, but real care for the horse is missing.
core_idea: Good intentions are not the same as real care

text: In the State of Sung there is a place called Ching-shih, where thrive the beech, the cedar, and the mulberry. Such as are of a one-handed span or so in girth are cut down for monkey-cages. Those of two or three two-handed spans are cut down for the beams of fine houses. Those of seven or eight such spans are cut down for the solid sides of rich men's coffins. Thus they do not fulfil their allotted span of years, but perish in mid-career beneath the axe. Such is the misfortune which overtakes worth.
note: Being used up because of your usefulness

tags.when_helps: Someone exploited for their talents who wonders about the cost of being useful.

display_text: In the State of Sung there is a place called Ching-shih, where thrive the beech, the cedar, and the mulberry. Such as are of a one-handed span or so in girth are cut down for monkey-cages. Those of two or three two-handed spans are cut down for the beams of fine houses. Those of seven or eight such spans are cut down for the solid sides of rich men's coffins. Thus they do not fulfil their allotted span of years, but perish in mid-career beneath the axe. Such is the misfortune which overtakes worth.
plain: Trees of every size are cut down for useful things: monkey cages, house beams, rich men's coffins. So they never live out their years. Being valuable brings this misfortune.
core_idea: Being useful can cut your life short

text: The honours of this world are light as feathers, yet none estimate them at their true value. The misfortunes of this life are weighty as the earth itself, yet none can keep out of their reach.
note: Status matters less than we think; misfortune comes to all

tags.when_helps: Someone chasing honours while burdened by hardship, wanting perspective on both.

display_text: The honours of this world are light as feathers, yet none estimate them at their true value. The misfortunes of this life are weighty as the earth itself, yet none can keep out of their reach.
plain: The honours of this world weigh as little as feathers, yet nobody sees how little they are worth. The troubles of life weigh as much as the earth, yet nobody can escape them.
core_idea: Honours are light; misfortunes are heavy and unavoidable

text: Those with toes who laugh at me for having no toes are many. This used to make me angry. But since I have studied under our Master, I have ceased to trouble about it. It may be that our Master has so far succeeded in purifying me. At any rate I have been with him nineteen years without being aware of the loss of my toes.
note: Being mocked for a disability; letting go of anger

tags.when_helps: Someone mocked for a disability or difference who wants to stop being troubled by it.

display_text: Those with toes who laugh at me for having no toes are many. This used to make me angry. But since I have studied under our Master, I have ceased to trouble about it. It may be that our Master has so far succeeded in purifying me. At any rate I have been with him nineteen years without being aware of the loss of my toes.
plain: Many people with toes laughed at me for having none, and it used to make me angry. Since studying with our Master I no longer care; I have been with him nineteen years without even noticing the missing toes.
core_idea: Inner growth makes others' mockery stop mattering

plain_judge.issue: Drops his suggestion that the Master has purified him.

text: He who knows what God is, and who knows what Man is, has attained. Knowing what God is, he knows that he himself proceeded therefrom. Knowing what Man is, he rests in the knowledge of the known, waiting for the knowledge of the unknown. Working out one's allotted span, and not perishing in mid career,--this is the fulness of knowledge.
note: Resting in what you know; patience with the unknown

tags.when_helps: Someone seeking to understand their place in the universe and live out their days well.

display_text: He who knows what God is, and who knows what Man is, has attained. Knowing what God is, he knows that he himself proceeded therefrom. Knowing what Man is, he rests in the knowledge of the known, waiting for the knowledge of the unknown. Working out one's allotted span, and not perishing in mid career,--this is the fulness of knowledge.
plain: Whoever knows what God is and what Man is has arrived: he knows he came from God, rests in what is known, and waits for the unknown. Living out your full span is the fullness of knowledge.
core_idea: Knowing God and Man, rest and live your span

text: The pure men of old acted without calculation, not seeking to secure results. They laid no plans. Therefore, failing, they had no cause for regret; succeeding, no cause for congratulation.
note: Freedom from regret by not clinging to results

tags.when_helps: Someone over-planning and fretting about results who needs release from attachment to outcomes.

display_text: The pure men of old acted without calculation, not seeking to secure results. They laid no plans. Therefore, failing, they had no cause for regret; succeeding, no cause for congratulation.
plain: The pure people of old acted without scheming and didn't chase results. They made no plans, so when they failed they had nothing to regret, and when they succeeded nothing to boast about.
core_idea: Acting without scheming leaves no regret or pride

text: The pure men of old slept without dreams, and waked without anxiety. They ate without discrimination, breathing deep breaths. For pure men draw breath from their uttermost depths; the vulgar only from their throats.
note: Calm, anxiety-free living; deep breathing

tags.when_helps: A person sleeping badly and breathing shallow with worry, looking for an image of calm, rooted living.

display_text: The pure men of old slept without dreams, and waked without anxiety. They ate without discrimination, breathing deep breaths. For pure men draw breath from their uttermost depths; the vulgar only from their throats.
plain: The pure people of old slept without dreams and woke without worry. They ate whatever came and breathed deeply, for the pure breathe from their very depths, while common people breathe only from their throats.
core_idea: The pure live calmly and breathe from deep within

text: The pure men of old did not know what it was to love life or to hate death. They did not rejoice in birth, nor strive to put off dissolution. Quickly come, and quickly go;--no more. They did not forget whence it was they had sprung, neither did they seek to hasten their return thither. Cheerfully they played their allotted parts, waiting patiently for the end.
note: Equanimity about life and death

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of dying or ageing who needs a calm, accepting view of life's natural span.

display_text: The pure men of old did not know what it was to love life or to hate death. They did not rejoice in birth, nor strive to put off dissolution. Quickly come, and quickly go;--no more. They did not forget whence it was they had sprung, neither did they seek to hasten their return thither. Cheerfully they played their allotted parts, waiting patiently for the end.
plain: The pure people of old neither loved life nor hated death; they came and went. Not forgetting their origin, nor rushing back to it, they cheerfully played their parts and waited patiently for the end.
core_idea: Live your part cheerfully, neither clinging nor rushing

text: When the pond dries up, and the fishes are left upon dry ground, to moisten them with the breath or to damp them with spittle is not to be compared with leaving them in the first instance in their native rivers and lakes. And better than praising Yao and blaming Chieh would be leaving them both and attending to the development of TAO.
note: Prevention over rescue; letting people live naturally

situations: loss of a home or something valued
tags.when_helps: Someone stranded outside their natural element, propped up by small comforts, reflecting on where they truly belong.

display_text: When the pond dries up, and the fishes are left upon dry ground, to moisten them with the breath or to damp them with spittle is not to be compared with leaving them in the first instance in their native rivers and lakes. And better than praising Yao and blaming Chieh would be leaving them both and attending to the development of TAO.
plain: Wetting stranded fish with breath or spit is nothing compared with leaving them in their rivers to begin with. Likewise, better than praising good rulers and blaming bad ones is to leave both and develop the Tao.
core_idea: Better to live naturally in the Tao than be rescued

text: TAO gives me this form, this toil in manhood, this repose in old age, this rest in death. And surely that which is such a kind arbiter of my life is the best arbiter of my death.
note: Ageing and death; trusting the course of life

tags.safety_reason: Presents death as rest decided by a kind arbiter, which a distressed reader could take as death being a welcome release.
tags.when_helps: An older reader at peace with life's seasons, wanting to trust that death belongs to a kindly order.

display_text: TAO gives me this form, this toil in manhood, this repose in old age, this rest in death. And surely that which is such a kind arbiter of my life is the best arbiter of my death.
plain: The Tao gives me my body, my work as an adult, my rest in old age, and my rest in death. Whatever arranges my life so kindly is also the best judge of my death.
core_idea: Trust the Tao that shapes your life with your death

text: To have attained to the human form must be always a source of joy. And then, to undergo countless transitions, with only the infinite to look forward to,--what incomparable bliss is that!
note: Joy in being alive; welcoming change

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling wonder at being alive who wants to celebrate the human form and endless change.

display_text: To have attained to the human form must be always a source of joy. And then, to undergo countless transitions, with only the infinite to look forward to,--what incomparable bliss is that!
plain: Being born human is always a reason for joy. And then to go through countless changes, with only the infinite ahead of you, is a happiness beyond compare.
core_idea: Being human, and endlessly changing, is great joy

text: Suppose that the boiling metal in a smelting-pot were to bubble up and say, 'Make of me an Excalibur;' I think the caster would reject that metal as uncanny. text: The ruler of the southern sea was called Shu. The ruler of the northern sea was called Hu. The ruler of the central zone was called Hun Tun. text: He who would attain to such perfection never loses sight of the natural conditions of his existence. With him the joined is not united, nor the separated apart, nor the long in excess, nor the short wanting. For just as a duck's legs, though short, cannot be lengthened without pain to the duck, and a crane's legs, though long, cannot be shortened without misery to the crane, so that which is long in man's moral nature cannot be cut off, nor that which is short be lengthened. All sorrow is thus avoided.
note: Accepting your own nature instead of forcing change

tags.when_helps: Someone trying to change their basic nature to fit others, who needs permission to stay as they are.

display_text: He who would attain to such perfection never loses sight of the natural conditions of his existence. text: What I call perfection of hearing is not hearing others but oneself. What I call perfection of vision is not seeing others but oneself. tags.when_helps: Someone so focused on others that they have lost themselves, needing to turn their attention inward.

display_text: What I call perfection of hearing is not hearing others but oneself. What I call perfection of vision is not seeing others but oneself. core_idea: Watch yourself, not others, to stay yourself

text: For all men strive to grasp what they do not know, while none strive to grasp what they already know; and all strive to discredit what they do not excel in, while none strive to discredit what they do excel in.

display_text: For all men strive to grasp what they do not know, while none strive to grasp what they already know; and all strive to discredit what they do not excel in, while none strive to discredit what they do excel in.
plain: Everyone strains to grasp what they don't know, but no one works on what they already know; and everyone runs down what they aren't good at, but no one questions what they are good at.
core_idea: People chase the unknown and dismiss what they lack

text: When man rejoices greatly he gravitates towards the positive pole. When he sorrows deeply he gravitates towards the negative pole. If the equilibrium of positive and negative is disturbed, the four seasons are interrupted, the balance of heat and cold is destroyed, and man himself suffers physically thereby. Because men are made to rejoice and to sorrow and to displace their centre of gravity, they lose their steadiness, and are unsuccessful in thought and action.
note: Emotional extremes throw us off balance

tags.when_helps: Someone swinging between highs and lows who wants to understand why balance matters to body and mind.

display_text: When man rejoices greatly he gravitates towards the positive pole. When he sorrows deeply he gravitates towards the negative pole. plain: Great joy pulls a person to one extreme, deep sorrow to the other, and when that balance is upset, nature and the body suffer. Swung between joy and sorrow, people lose their steadiness and fail in thought and action.

text: By gentleness, the hardest heart may be softened. But try to cut and polish it,--'twill glow like fire or freeze like ice. In the twinkling of an eye it will pass beyond the limits of the Four Seas. In repose, profoundly still; in motion, far away in the sky. No bolt can bar, no bond can bind,--such is the human heart.
note: Gentleness versus force with a restless human heart

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone dealing with a hardened heart, their own or another's, wondering whether force or gentleness works.

display_text: By gentleness, the hardest heart may be softened. But try to cut and polish it,--'twill glow like fire or freeze like ice. plain: Gentleness can soften the hardest heart, but try to cut and shape it and it blazes or freezes. In an instant it reaches the ends of the earth; nothing can lock or bind it. Such is the human heart.
core_idea: The human heart yields to gentleness, never to force

text: See nothing; hear nothing; let your soul be wrapped in quiet; and your body will begin to take proper form. Let there be absolute repose and absolute purity; do not weary your body nor disturb your vitality,--and you will live for ever.

plain: See nothing and hear nothing; let your soul rest in quiet, and your body will take its proper shape. Keep total stillness and purity, don't tire your body or disturb your energy, and you will live for ever.
core_idea: Deep stillness and purity preserve body and soul

text: Cherish that which is within you, and shut off that which is without; for much knowledge is a curse.

display_text: Cherish that which is within you, and shut off that which is without; for much knowledge is a curse.

core_idea: Guard your inner life; much knowledge is a curse

text: Rest in inaction, and the world will be good of itself. Cast your slough. Spit forth intelligence. Ignore all differences. Become one with the infinite. Release your mind. Free your soul. Be vacuous. Be Nothing!

core_idea: Let go of doing and cleverness; become one with all

text: The men of this world all rejoice in others being like themselves, and object to others not being like themselves. text: Movement and rest, life and death, rise and fall, are not at the beck and call of man. Cultivation of self is in his own hands.

core_idea: Life's events aren't yours to control; self-cultivation is

text: If you tell a man he is a wheedler, he will not like it. If you tell him he is a flatterer, he will be angry. Yet he is everlastingly both. But all such sham and pretence is what the world likes, and consequently people do not punish each other for doing what they do themselves. For a man to arrange his dress, or make a display, or suit his expression so as to get into the good graces of the world, and yet not to call himself a flatterer; to identify himself in every way with the yeas and nays of his fellows, and yet not call himself one of them;--this is the height of folly.

tags.when_helps: Someone bending themselves to win approval who is ready to see the folly of pretence.

display_text: If you tell a man he is a wheedler, he will not like it. If you tell him he is a flatterer, he will be angry. Yet he is everlastingly both. text: The repose of the Sage is not what the world calls repose. His repose is the result of his mental attitude. All creation could not disturb his equilibrium: hence his repose. display_text: When Hsi Shih was distressed in mind, she knitted her brows. display_text: Those who make wealth their all in all, cannot bear loss of money. Those who make distinction their all in all, cannot bear loss of fame. display_text: Of old, attainment of desire did not mean office. It meant that nothing could be added to the sum of happiness. text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,--the creature of a season. You cannot speak of TAO to a pedagogue: his scope is too restricted.

text: Dimensions are limitless; time is endless. Conditions are not invariable; terms are not final. He looks back into the past, and does not grieve over what is far off, nor rejoice over what is near; for he knows that time is without end. He investigates fulness and decay, and does not rejoice if he succeeds, nor lament if he fails; for he knows that conditions are not invariable. text: Chuang Tzŭ was fishing in the P'u when the prince of Ch'u sent two high officials to ask him to take charge of the administration of the Ch'u State. text: When Chuang Tzŭ's wife died, Hui Tzŭ went to condole. He found the widower sitting on the ground, singing, with his legs spread out at a right angle, and beating time on a bowl. "To live with your wife," exclaimed Hui Tzŭ, "and see your eldest son grow up to be a man, and then not to shed a tear over her corpse,--this would be bad enough. But to drum on a bowl, and sing; surely this is going too far." "Not at all," replied Chuang Tzŭ. "When she died, I could not help being affected by her death. Soon, however, I remembered that she had already existed in a previous state before birth, without form, or even substance; that while in that unconditioned condition, substance was added to spirit; that this substance then assumed form; and that the next stage was birth. And now, by virtue of a further change, she is dead, passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. And while she is thus lying asleep in Eternity, for me to go about weeping and wailing would be to proclaim myself ignorant of these natural laws. Therefore I refrain."

tags.when_helps: A bereaved person who has begun to look past raw grief and wants to see death within nature's cycle.

text: Suppose a boat is crossing a river, and another empty boat is about to collide with it. Even an irritable man would not lose his temper. But supposing there was some one in the second boat. display_text: The universe is very beautiful, yet it says nothing. The four seasons abide by a fixed law, yet they are not heard. All creation is based upon absolute principles, yet nothing speaks.
plain: The universe is deeply beautiful yet says nothing. The seasons follow a fixed law yet make no sound. All creation rests on absolute principles, yet nothing speaks.
core_idea: The universe's beauty and order are silent

text: Keep your body under proper control, your gaze concentrated upon ONE,--and the peace of God will descend upon you. Keep back your knowledge, and concentrate your thoughts upon ONE,--and the holy spirit shall abide within you.
note: Stillness and focus in meditation

tags.when_helps: Someone with a scattered mind seeking a simple practice of focus that brings peace.

display_text: Keep your body under proper control, your gaze concentrated upon ONE,--and the peace of God will descend upon you. Keep back your knowledge, and concentrate your thoughts upon ONE,--and the holy spirit shall abide within you.
plain: Keep your body disciplined and your gaze fixed on the One, and the peace of God will come down on you. Hold back your knowledge and focus your thoughts on the One, and the holy spirit will live within you.
core_idea: Focus on the One and God's peace comes

text: "Man passes through this sublunary life as a white horse passes a crack. Here one moment, gone the next. Neither are there any not equally subject to the ingress and egress of mortality. One modification brings life; then another, and it is death. Living creatures cry out; human beings sorrow. The bow-sheath is slipped off; the clothes-bag is dropped; and in the confusion the soul wings its flight, and the body follows, on the great journey home!
note: Brevity of life; facing death

tags.safety_reason: Frames death as the soul's great journey home, which a distressed reader could take as a welcome release.
tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on the brevity of life and the mystery of death, not in acute distress.

display_text: Man passes through this sublunary life as a white horse passes a crack. Here one moment, gone the next. Neither are there any not equally subject to the ingress and egress of mortality. One modification brings life; then another, and it is death. Living creatures cry out; human beings sorrow. plain: A human life passes like a white horse glimpsed through a crack: here, then gone. One change brings life, another death; creatures cry out and people grieve. Then the soul takes flight and the body follows on the journey home.
core_idea: Life flashes past; death is the journey home

text: The man who forged swords for the Minister of War was eighty years of age. Yet he never made the slightest slip in his work. The Minister of War said to him, "Is it your skill, Sir, or have you any method?" "It is concentration," replied the man. "When twenty years old, I took to forging swords. I cared for nothing else. If a thing was not a sword, I did not notice it. I availed myself of whatever energy I did not use in other directions in order to secure greater efficiency in the direction required.
note: Focus and mastery in one's work

tags.when_helps: Someone scattered across many interests who wants to master one craft through focus.

core_idea: Mastery comes from total, lifelong concentration

text: Let your modification extend to the external only. Internally, be constant without modification.
note: Adapting outwardly while staying true inwardly

tags.when_helps: Someone adapting to outside pressures who needs to stay steady within while flexing outwardly.

display_text: Let your modification extend to the external only. Internally, be constant without modification.
plain: Let yourself change only on the outside. On the inside, stay constant and unchanged.
core_idea: Adapt outwardly; stay constant within

text: "Mountain forests and loamy fields swell my heart with joy. But ere the joy be passed, sorrow is upon me again. Joy and sorrow come and go, and over them I have no control. "Alas! the life of man is but as a stoppage at an inn. He knows that which comes within the range of his experience. Otherwise, he knows not. He knows that he can do what he can do, and that he cannot do what he cannot do. But there is always that which he does not know and that which he cannot do; and to struggle that it shall not be so,--is not this a cause for grief?
note: Changing moods; accepting human limits

tags.when_helps: Someone saddened that joy keeps giving way to sorrow and that so much lies beyond their power.

core_idea: Fighting life's limits only brings more grief

text: "If I do not know," replied Nan Yung, "men call me a fool. If I do know, I injure myself. If I am not charitable, I injure others. If I am, I injure myself. If I do not do my duty to my neighbour, I injure others. If I do it, I injure myself. My trouble lies in not seeing how to escape from these three dilemmas. On the strength of my connection with Kêng Sang, I would venture to ask advice." "When I saw you," said Lao Tzŭ, "I knew in the twinkling of an eye what was the matter with you. And now what you say confirms my view. You are confused, as a child that has lost its parents. You would fathom the sea with a pole. You are astray. You are struggling to get back to your natural self, but cannot find the way. Alas! alas!"
note: Feeling trapped by dilemmas; lost from oneself

tags.when_helps: Someone caught in no-win dilemmas, confused and astray, struggling to find their way back to themselves.

core_idea: Lost in dilemmas, he can't find his natural self

plain_judge.issue: Collapses the three specific dilemmas (knowledge, charity, duty) into a general statement.

text: "If the disturbances are external, do not be always combating them, but close the channels to the mind. If the disturbances are internal, do not strive to oppose them, but close all entrance from without.
note: Dealing with inner and outer turmoil

tags.when_helps: Someone besieged by outer or inner disturbances who wants practical counsel to stop fighting them.

display_text: If the disturbances are external, do not be always combating them, but close the channels to the mind. If the disturbances are internal, do not strive to oppose them, but close all entrance from without.
plain: If the trouble comes from outside, don't keep fighting it; close the paths into your mind. If it comes from inside, don't struggle against it; shut out everything from outside.
core_idea: Don't fight disturbances; close the way in

text: "The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, to lose nothing, to estimate good and evil without divination, to know when to stop, and how much is enough, to leave others alone and attend to oneself, to be without cares and without knowledge,--to be in fact as a child.
note: Contentment, knowing enough, childlike simplicity

tags.when_helps: Someone overcomplicating life who wants a simple rule: know when to stop and how much is enough.

display_text: The art of preserving life," replied Lao Tzŭ, "consists in being able to keep all in ONE, to lose nothing, to estimate good and evil without divination, to know when to stop, and how much is enough, to leave others alone and attend to oneself, to be without cares and without knowledge,--to be in fact as a child.
plain: Lao Tzu said that preserving life means keeping all in the One, losing nothing, knowing when to stop and what is enough, minding your own affairs, being free of cares and cleverness: in fact, being like a child.
core_idea: To preserve life, be simple like a child

text: "Those whose hearts are in a state of repose give forth a divine radiance, by the light of which they see themselves as they are. And only by cultivating such repose can man attain to the constant.
note: Inner calm and self-knowledge

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to see themselves clearly, drawn to the idea that inner repose brings light.

display_text: Those whose hearts are in a state of repose give forth a divine radiance, by the light of which they see themselves as they are. And only by cultivating such repose can man attain to the constant.
plain: People whose hearts are at rest give off a divine light, by which they see themselves as they really are. Only by cultivating that inner rest can anyone reach what is constant.
core_idea: A restful heart lets you see yourself truly

text: Those who are devoted to the internal, in practice acquire no reputation. Those who are devoted to the external, strive for pre-eminence among their fellows. Practice without reputation throws a halo around the meanest. But he who strives for pre-eminence among his fellows, he is as a huckster whose weariness all perceive though he himself puts on an air of gaiety.
note: Chasing status versus quiet inner work

tags.when_helps: Someone whose quiet inner work goes unnoticed while showier people get ahead.

display_text: Those who are devoted to the internal, in practice acquire no reputation. Those who are devoted to the external, strive for pre-eminence among their fellows. Practice without reputation throws a halo around the meanest. But he who strives for pre-eminence among his fellows, he is as a huckster whose weariness all perceive though he himself puts on an air of gaiety.
plain: Those devoted to inner life gain no reputation; those devoted to outward things compete for the top. Quiet practice makes even the humblest shine, while the status-seeker is like a peddler whose tiredness shows through his forced cheer.
core_idea: Quiet inner practice shines; chasing status shows strain

text: "There is no weapon so deadly as man's will. Excalibur is second to it. There is no bandit so powerful as Nature. In the whole universe there is no escape from it. Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart.
note: Suffering caused by one's own heart

tags.when_helps: Someone blaming fate or circumstance who could see that the real harm comes from one's own heart.

display_text: There is no weapon so deadly as man's will. Excalibur is second to it. There is no bandit so powerful as Nature. In the whole universe there is no escape from it. Yet it is not Nature which does the injury. It is man's own heart.
plain: No weapon is as deadly as human will, and no bandit as powerful as Nature, which nothing in the universe escapes. Yet it is not Nature that does the harm; it is a person's own heart.
core_idea: Harm comes from our own heart, not Nature

text: "Birth is not a beginning; death is not an end. There is existence without limitation; there is continuity without a starting-point.
note: Death and continuity

tags.when_helps: Someone fearing death as final who is comforted by a vision of continuous existence.

display_text: Birth is not a beginning; death is not an end. There is existence without limitation; there is continuity without a starting-point.
plain: Birth is not a beginning, and death is not an end. There is existence without limit and continuity without a starting point.
core_idea: Birth doesn't begin us; death doesn't end us

text: "If you would attain peace, level down your emotional nature. If you desire spirituality, cultivate adaptation of the intelligence. If you would have your actions in accordance with what is right, allow yourself to fall in with the dictates of necessity. For necessity is the TAO of the Sage."
note: Finding peace; accepting necessity

tags.when_helps: Someone tossed by strong emotions seeking peace by leveling them and accepting necessity.

display_text: "If you would attain peace, level down your emotional nature. If you desire spirituality, cultivate adaptation of the intelligence. If you would have your actions in accordance with what is right, allow yourself to fall in with the dictates of necessity. For necessity is the TAO of the Sage."
plain: If you want peace, calm your emotions. If you want spirituality, let your mind adapt. If you want to act rightly, go along with what is necessary, because necessity is the sage's Tao.
core_idea: Calm emotions, adapt, and accept necessity

text: "Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. After a month, he was glad to meet any one he had even seen there. And after a year, he was glad to meet any one who was in any way like to his fellow-countrymen. Is not this a case of absence from one's kind increasing the desire to be with them?
note: Loneliness, exile, longing for one's people

tags.when_helps: Someone long cut off from their own people, feeling how absence sharpens the hunger for company.

display_text: Have you not heard," said Hsü Wu Kuei, "of the outlaw of Yüeh? After several days' absence from his State, he was glad to meet any one he had known there. plain: An exile is glad after days to meet anyone he knew from home, after a month anyone he'd seen there, after a year anyone resembling his countrymen. Being away from your own kind makes you long for them more.
core_idea: Absence from your own kind deepens the longing

text: "Being high up does not make one high, nor does being low make one low.
note: Status does not define worth

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling small because of a low position, reminded that rank does not set worth.

display_text: Being high up does not make one high, nor does being low make one low.
plain: Being in a high position doesn't make you a great person, and being in a low one doesn't make you a lesser one.
core_idea: Rank does not make anyone high or low

text: If schemers have nothing to give them anxiety, they are not happy. If dialecticians have not their premisses and conclusion, they are not happy. If critics have none on whom to vent their spleen, they are not happy. Such men are the slaves of objective existences.
note: Restlessness; dependence on outside things for happiness

tags.when_helps: Someone who only feels alive when scheming or criticising, ready to see that dependence.

display_text: If schemers have nothing to give them anxiety, they are not happy. If dialecticians have not their premisses and conclusion, they are not happy. If critics have none on whom to vent their spleen, they are not happy. Such men are the slaves of objective existences.
plain: Schemers aren't happy without something to worry about, debaters without their arguments, critics without someone to attack. Such people are slaves to things outside themselves.
core_idea: Needing outside things to be happy is slavery

text: Take away agriculture from the husbandman, and his classification is gone. Take away trade from the merchant, and his classification is gone. Daily work is the stimulus of the labourer. The skill of the artisan is his pride. If money cannot be made, the avaricious man is sad. If his power meets with a check, the boaster will repine. Ambitious men love change. Thus, men are always doing something; inaction is to them impossible. They observe in this the same regularity as the seasons, ever without change. They hurry to destruction, dissipating in all directions their vital forces, alas! never to return.
note: Identity tied to work; restless busyness

tags.when_helps: Someone always busy and striving who is beginning to sense the cost of never stopping.

display_text: Take away agriculture from the husbandman, and his classification is gone. Take away trade from the merchant, and his classification is gone. Daily work is the stimulus of the labourer. plain: Farmers, merchants, workers, the greedy, the boastful and the ambitious all depend on their activity; without it they are lost. People can never stop doing, and so they rush to ruin, scattering their life energy for good.
core_idea: Endless restless doing drains life away

text: "He who would seek for a stray child, but will not leave his home, is like to lose him.
note: Needing to act, not just wish

tags.when_helps: Someone searching for something while refusing to leave their comfort zone.

display_text: He who would seek for a stray child, but will not leave his home, is like to lose him.
plain: Anyone who wants to find a lost child but won't leave the house is likely to lose the child.
core_idea: You can't find what's lost without leaving home

text: Chuang Tzŭ was once attending a funeral, when he passed by the grave of Hui Tzŭ. Turning to his attendants, he said, "A man of Ying who had his nose covered with a hard scab, no thicker than a fly's wing, sent for a stone-mason to chip it off. The stone-mason plied his adze with great dexterity while the patient sat still and let him chip. When the scab was all off, the nose was found to be uninjured, the man of Ying never having moved a muscle. "When Yüan, prince of Sung, heard of this, he summoned the stone-mason and said, 'Try to do the same for me.' "'I used to be able to do it Sire,' replied the stone-mason, 'but my material has long since perished.' "And I too, ever since he perished, have been without my material, having no one with whom I can speak."
note: Grief for a lost friend and companion

tags.when_helps: Someone who has lost the one friend who truly understood them and now has no one to talk with.

text: "To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom. To share one's wealth with others is reckoned meritorious. To exhibit superior merit is not the way to win men's hearts. To exhibit inferior merit is the way.
note: Humility and generosity win hearts

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to win others over who could learn that modesty works better than display.

display_text: To share one's virtue with others is called true wisdom. To share one's wealth with others is reckoned meritorious. To exhibit superior merit is not the way to win men's hearts. To exhibit inferior merit is the way.
plain: Sharing your virtue with others is true wisdom; sharing your wealth is counted as merit. Showing off your superiority doesn't win people's hearts; showing yourself as lesser does.
core_idea: Humility, not displayed superiority, wins hearts

text: The prince of Wu took a boat and went to the Monkey Mountain, which he ascended. When the monkeys saw him, they fled in terror and hid themselves in the thicket. One of them, however, disported himself carelessly, as though showing off its skill before the prince. The prince took a shot at it; but the monkey, with great rapidity, seized the flying arrow with its hand. Then the prince bade his guards try, the result being that the monkey was killed. Thereupon the prince turned to his friend Yen Pu I, and said, "That monkey flaunted its skill and its dexterity in my face. Therefore it has come to this pass. Beware! Do not flaunt your superiority in the faces of others."
note: Danger of showing off and arrogance

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to flaunt their skill or success in front of others.

core_idea: Flaunting your superiority invites destruction

text: "A dog is not considered a good dog because he is a good barker. A man is not considered a good man because he is a good talker. How much less in the case of greatness? And if doing great things is not enough to secure greatness, how much less shall it secure virtue?
note: Talk and achievement are not goodness

tags.when_helps: Someone relying on talk or achievements to prove worth, reminded that goodness is something deeper.

display_text: A dog is not considered a good dog because he is a good barker. A man is not considered a good man because he is a good talker. How much less in the case of greatness? And if doing great things is not enough to secure greatness, how much less shall it secure virtue?
plain: A dog isn't good just because it barks well, nor a person good just because he talks well. Greatness needs even more than that; and if doing great things doesn't make you great, it certainly doesn't make you virtuous.
core_idea: Talking well or doing great things isn't virtue

text: "Thus it has been said, 'The wind blows and the river suffers. The sun shines and the river suffers.' But though wind and sun be both brought into relation with the river, it does not really suffer therefrom. Fed from its source, it still continues to flow on.
note: Resilience under outside pressures

keywords: the river fed from its source
tags.when_helps: Someone battered by pressures who needs the image of a river that keeps flowing from its source.

display_text: Thus it has been said, 'The wind blows and the river suffers. The sun shines and the river suffers.' But though wind and sun be both brought into relation with the river, it does not really suffer therefrom. Fed from its source, it still continues to flow on.
plain: It is said that wind and sun make the river suffer. But though both act on it, the river is not really harmed: fed from its source, it keeps on flowing.
core_idea: Fed from its source, the river keeps flowing

text: "The foot treads the ground in walking; nevertheless it is the ground not trodden on which makes up the good walk. A man's knowledge is limited; but it is upon what he does not know that he depends to extend his knowledge to the apprehension of God.
note: Humility about the limits of knowledge

tags.when_helps: Someone humbled by how little they know, open to seeing the unknown as the way to the sacred.

display_text: The foot treads the ground in walking; nevertheless it is the ground not trodden on which makes up the good walk. A man's knowledge is limited; but it is upon what he does not know that he depends to extend his knowledge to the apprehension of God.
plain: Your foot touches only a little ground, yet it is the untrodden ground around it that makes walking possible. Human knowledge is limited, but it is on what we don't know that we rely to reach an understanding of God.
core_idea: The unknown is what leads us toward God

text: "The old country, the old home, gladden a wanderer's eyes. Nay, though nine-tenths of it be a howling wilderness, still his eye will be glad.
note: Homesickness; love for one's roots

situations: loss of a home or something valued
tags.when_helps: Someone far from home, longing for the familiar places of their past.

display_text: The old country, the old home, gladden a wanderer's eyes. Nay, though nine-tenths of it be a howling wilderness, still his eye will be glad.
plain: The old country and the old home delight a wanderer's eyes. Even if almost all of it has become a wilderness, his eyes are still glad to see it.
core_idea: Home gladdens the wanderer even in ruins

text: The true Sage ignores God. He ignores man. He ignores a beginning. He ignores matter. He moves in harmony with his generation and suffers not. He takes things as they come and is not overwhelmed. How are we to become like him?
note: Taking life as it comes without overwhelm

tags.when_helps: Someone overwhelmed by events who wonders how to move in harmony with life and not suffer.

display_text: The true Sage ignores God. He ignores man. He ignores a beginning. He ignores matter. He moves in harmony with his generation and suffers not. He takes things as they come and is not overwhelmed. How are we to become like him?
plain: The true sage pays no attention to God, to man, to beginnings or to matter. He moves in step with his times without suffering and takes things as they come without being overwhelmed. How can we become like him?
core_idea: The sage takes things as they come, untroubled

text: "The rulers of old set off all success to the credit of their people, attributing all failure to themselves. All that was right went to the credit of their people, all that was wrong they attributed to themselves. Therefore, if any matter fell short of achievement, they turned and blamed themselves.
note: Leadership; taking responsibility for failure

tags.when_helps: A leader or manager tempted to blame others, considering how to own failures and share successes.

display_text: The rulers of old set off all success to the credit of their people, attributing all failure to themselves. All that was right went to the credit of their people, all that was wrong they attributed to themselves. Therefore, if any matter fell short of achievement, they turned and blamed themselves.
plain: The rulers of old gave their people credit for every success and took the blame for every failure. Whatever went right was the people's; whatever went wrong was theirs. So when anything fell short, they blamed themselves.
core_idea: Good leaders credit others and blame themselves

text: When Chü Poh Yü reached his sixtieth year, he changed his opinions. What he had previously regarded as right, he now came to regard as wrong. But who shall say whether the right of to-day may not be as wrong as the wrong of the previous fifty-nine years?
note: Changing one's mind with age; humility

tags.when_helps: Someone who has changed long-held beliefs and is unsure what to trust now.

display_text: When Chü Poh Yü reached his sixtieth year, he changed his opinions. What he had previously regarded as right, he now came to regard as wrong. But who shall say whether the right of to-day may not be as wrong as the wrong of the previous fifty-nine years?
plain: At sixty, Chü Poh Yü changed his mind, calling wrong what he had called right. But who can say today's right won't turn out as wrong as the views of his previous fifty-nine years?
core_idea: Today's certainty may be tomorrow's mistake

text: "Seasons have their beginnings and their ends. Generations change and change. Good and evil fortune alternate, bringing sorrow here, happiness there.
note: Ups and downs of fortune

tags.when_helps: Someone in a bad stretch who can take heart that fortune turns like the seasons.

display_text: Seasons have their beginnings and their ends. Generations change and change. Good and evil fortune alternate, bringing sorrow here, happiness there.
plain: Seasons begin and end. Generations keep changing. Good and bad fortune take turns, bringing sorrow in one place and happiness in another.
core_idea: Fortune and seasons turn; nothing stays

text: He who obstinately views things from his own standpoint only, may be right in one case and wrong in another.
note: Stubbornness and seeing other viewpoints

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone locked in an argument, ready to consider that their own view may be only partly right.

display_text: He who obstinately views things from his own standpoint only, may be right in one case and wrong in another.
plain: Someone who stubbornly sees things only from his own point of view may be right in one case and wrong in another.
core_idea: One fixed viewpoint is sometimes right, sometimes wrong

note: Cycles of fortune; endings bring renewal

tags.when_helps: Someone at a low ebb who could be steadied by the idea that exhaustion leads to renewal.

text: The States of Han and Wei were struggling to annex each other's territory when Tzŭ Hua Tzŭ went to see prince Chao Hsi. Finding the latter very downcast, Tzŭ Hua Tzŭ said, "Now suppose the representatives of the various States were to sign an agreement before your Highness, to the effect that although cutting off the left hand would involve loss of the right, while cutting off the right would involve loss of the left, nevertheless that whosoever would cut off either should be emperor over all,--would your Highness cut?" text: There was once a man who was so afraid of his shadow and so disliked his own footsteps that he determined to run away from them. But the oftener he raised his feet the more footsteps he made, and though he ran very hard his shadow never left him. From this he inferred that he went too slowly, and ran as hard as he could without resting, the consequence being that his strength broke down and he died. He was not aware that by going into the shade he would have got rid of his shadow, and that by keeping still he would have put an end to his footsteps. Fool that he was!
note: Running from oneself; anxiety eased by stillness

tags.when_helps: Someone running harder to escape their troubles, who might find relief by stopping and keeping still.

core_idea: Running from yourself only exhausts you; be still
